name: bddisasm
baseline: Capstone (decode+format throughput); Intel XED, diStorm, iced, yaxpeax-x86, Sleigh and the other listed decoders are measured in the same harness
workload: Decoding (and decoding plus formatting) the code section of a 64-bit x86 binary repeatedly in the disas-bench harness, reported as MB/s of machine code.
claimed_speedup: disas-bench charts (bar lengths measured against axis ticks, approximate): Ryzen 9 9950X: bddisasm decode+format 46.8 MB/s, bddisasm mini decode+format 48.8 MB/s, Capstone decode+format 27.5 MB/s; decode-only bddisasm 105.7 MB/s, bddisasm mini 179.3 MB/s. i9-13900K: bddisasm decode+format 35.6 MB/s, mini 39.0 MB/s, Capstone 25.9 MB/s; decode-only 102.7 MB/s, mini 179.5 MB/s. Decode+format ratio to Capstone 1.70x (AMD) and 1.37x (Intel), mini 1.77x and 1.51x (derived from page data, chart readings). README alone: legacy decoder around 240 CPU clocks per decoded instruction (~12M instructions/s) and mini decoder around 150 clocks (~17M instructions/s) on an Intel Core Ultra 7 165H with BDDISASM v3.0, no baseline.
compiler_and_flags: Harness binaries are built with cc -O3 (bench/cs/Makefile, bench/xed/Makefile, bench/bddisasm/Makefile; bench/zydis via CMake Release), GCC 13.3 on the AMD run and GCC 14.2 on the Intel run. Libraries: Capstone 5.0.6 (submodule accf4df) built with its own Makefile, default CFLAGS -O3, CAPSTONE_ARCHS=x86; bddisasm v3.0.0 via CMake Release with BDD_LTO=ON; Zydis via CMake Release (bench/zydis/CMakeLists.txt, submodule 569320a); XED via mfile.py --opt=3 (make-all.sh).
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 9950X (Ubuntu 24.04, Linux 6.8.0) and Intel Core i9-13900K (Debian trixie, Linux 6.12.48)
tradeoffs: C library with Python and Rust bindings, directly usable from C++. Includes a 'mini' decoder with reduced detail and a shellcode-detection emulator (not benchmarked). Decode+format advantage over Capstone is modest.
caveats: Smaller win than iced, yaxpeax-x86 and diStorm in the same charts (iced and yaxpeax decode+format are about 3.4-5.4x faster than bddisasm); the README's own throughput numbers carry no baseline. Each tool is timed in a single run (clock() CPU time over 20 passes of the 0x2460400-byte code section of a checked-in Firefox xul.dll), with no repetitions or variance reported. disas-bench is maintained by Joel Hoener (athre0z), a Zydis copyright holder; the AMD chart was produced by iximeow (yaxpeax-x86 author, 2025-10-24) and the Intel chart by athre0z (2025-10-26). Chart values are bar lengths read off PNGs against the axis ticks (approximate, about +/-1 MB/s), not a text table. Capstone appears only as a decode+format row (cs_disasm_iter, detail off), so decode+format rows are the like-for-like comparison; formatted text differs in detail between libraries. The bddisasm v3.0.0 update and the mini-decoder rows were contributed to disas-bench by ianichitei (2025-10-10), who also authored earlier bddisasm updates there.

name: diStorm3
baseline: Capstone, Zydis, Intel XED, bddisasm, udis86 and BeaEngine (other x86/x86-64 disassembler libraries)
workload: Decoding only, and decoding plus formatting, of the 77 MB .text section of Firefox 86.0.1's 64-bit xul.dll, throughput in MB/s (computed as bytes/1024/1024 per second). The README does not state the loop count: bench.py's built-in default is 20 passes over the 36.4 MiB section of the older 63 MB input/xul.dll checked into the repo, and with a custom file and no loop-count argument it scales the count to keep the same total bytes (about 9 passes over a 77 MB section, derived from bench.py). The Firefox 86 xul.dll itself is not in the repo.
claimed_speedup: Decode plus format: 58.85 MB/s versus Zydis 22.24, bddisasm 16.00, XED 15.67, Capstone 14.02, BeaEngine 13.42, udis86 12.02 MB/s (about 4.2x Capstone, derived from page data); second only to iced (149.21). Decode only: 92.17 MB/s versus XED 55.39, Zydis (min) 61.33, bddisasm 35.48, Zydis 34.19, udis86 80.72 MB/s.
compiler_and_flags: Kubuntu 21.04, gcc 10.3.0, Rust 1.52.1 (disas-bench README). make-all.sh builds the C libraries with gcc and LTO: Capstone and bddisasm as CMake Release builds with CFLAGS=-flto, XED via mfile.py --opt=3 --extra-flags=-flto, diStorm via its own make/linux Makefile (current version: -fPIC -O2 -std=c99) with -flto prepended, BeaEngine patched to -O3 -flto, udis86 without LTO (it got slower). The C bench drivers (bench/*/Makefile) are built with -flto -O3; the Zydis driver is a CMake Release build with CFLAGS=-flto. The Rust drivers (bench/iced-x86/Cargo.toml, bench/yaxpeax/Cargo.toml) use a release profile with opt-level=3, lto=true, codegen-units=1 and no target-cpu setting. C libraries and yaxpeax-x86 are pinned git submodules (last updated March 2021); iced is pulled unpinned from its git master at build time.
tradeoffs: Plain C with a single API (about 45 KB per its README), callable directly from C++. Decodes x86/AMD64 only; coverage of recent instruction-set extensions was not checked.
caveats: Numbers are from the iced author's disas-bench fork (June 2021, i5-6600K) with the diStorm submodule of March 2021; diStorm's last commit is 2021-12-18 (v3.5.3), so it is abandoned and instruction-set coverage added since then by other decoders was not checked. The decode+format driver discards distorm_format64's output, but its time is well above decode-only (58.85 vs 92.17 MB/s), so formatting work is being timed. Formatters differ in output syntax between libraries. The yaxpeax author's later fork (i7-12700K, GCC 11, rustc 1.67 nightly, bar chart without numbers) shows diStorm at roughly 138 MB/s decode and 86 MB/s decode+format, still ahead of Capstone, XED, Zydis and bddisasm but behind iced and yaxpeax (values read off the bars, approximate). Figure 11 plots speedups over llvm -O0 for Hacker's Delight p01-p25, saxpy, mont and list; per-kernel values appear only in the chart. Correctness is checked on at most 10 CodeNet test inputs per program, and timings are whole-process (startup included) on small competitive-programming programs, run concurrently in a thread pool. The output is a fine-tuned model (HuggingFace LLM4Code/Superoptimizer_Qwen7B, licence not checked), not a library; the repo is a 2-commit code drop. Preprint status.

name: SLOTHY
baseline: unscheduled 'clean' hand-written assembly and prior hand-optimized implementations of the same kernels (ML-KEM and ML-DSA NTTs, FFT, X25519); no compiler baseline stated on the pages opened
workload: Instruction scheduling, register allocation and software pipelining of hand-written Arm AArch64, Armv8.1-M and RISC-V assembly for cryptographic and DSP kernels.
claimed_speedup: README: SLOTHY has been used 'to provide the fastest known implementations of various cryptographic and DSP primitives' (ML-KEM and ML-DSA NTTs for Cortex-A55/A72/M55/M85, FFT for Cortex-M55/M85, X25519 for Cortex-A55); no speedup numbers on any page opened. Related adoption number: the AWS-LC pull request that imported the s2n-bignum X25519 rewrite (partly SLOTHY-generated) reports 12867.1 to 22361.9 ops/sec ('74% speedup') on Graviton 2, but that gain is not attributable to SLOTHY alone.
hardware: Targets Cortex-M55, M85, A55 (supported), A72, Cortex-X/Neoverse-V, Apple M1 (experimental) and XuanTie C908
stars_or_usage: 352 stars; adopted in AWS-LC / s2n-bignum, Arm EndpointAI CMSIS DSP and mlkem-native
tradeoffs: Microarchitecture-specific by design: each output is scheduled for one core model (portability note: code tuned for Cortex-A55 is not tuned for other cores). Solver time is seconds to minutes for under 50 instructions and minutes to hours for up to 150 instructions; larger kernels need heuristics. Python tool using Google OR-Tools.
caveats: The TCHES 2024 paper 'Fast and Clean: Auditable high-performance assembly via constraint solving' (issue 1, pp. 87-132, artifact at artifacts.iacr.org/tches/2024/a6; eprint 2022/1303) is peer-reviewed but could not be opened (tches.iacr.org and eprint unreachable); WebSearch snippets only say the SLOTHY-optimized code matches or beats prior art in all cases, with no cycle counts. The repo ships clean and optimized sources (paper/clean, paper/opt), optimization scripts (paper/scripts) and a Docker artifact; cycle benchmarks live in pqax/pqmx and need Cortex-A55/A72 devices or an MPS3 FPGA board (AN547/AN555), and builds without CYCLES=PMU/PERF stub out cycle counts. The only number in the repo is the tutorial's LLVM-MCA model estimate for a toy Cortex-A55 loop (31 to 21 cycles per iteration), a model output against its own unscheduled input, not a measurement. Adoption is real: s2n-bignum PR #108 (merged 2024-02-15) imported the SLOTHY-generated Lenngren-based X25519 without benchmark numbers; the AWS-LC PR #1469 that reports 12867.1 to 22361.9 ops/sec ('74% speedup', Graviton 2) was closed without merge on 2024-03-06 (the README calls it merged) and mixes the algorithm change with SLOTHY scheduling. CP-SAT is non-deterministic, so re-optimization results vary, especially for the heuristic Cortex-A72 model. SLOTHY is a Python tool that produces assembly; it is not linked into the user's program.

name: positional-popcount
baseline: pospopcnt_u16_scalar_naive (portable scalar C, auto-vectorized by GCC) and pospopcnt_u16_scalar_naive_nosimd
workload: Positional population count (set-bit counts at each of 16 bit positions) over arrays of 16-bit values; the speedup tables cover arrays of 128 to 65536 values on one core, while the cycles-per-integer and MB/s tables use 1 million uniformly random simulated FLAG fields over 1,000 repetitions.
claimed_speedup: pospopcnt_u16_avx512_harley_seal is 16.28x faster than the auto-vectorized scalar naive version at 65536 values (6.43x at 4096, 9.41x at 8192) and 138.71x faster than the no-SIMD naive version at 65536 values; AVX-512 adder forest 4.96x at 2048; at 128 values the Harley-Seal version is 0.52x (slower). README also states about 50 GB/s (about 0.120 cycles per 16-bit integer) with AVX-512.
compiler_and_flags: gcc (GCC) 7.3.1 20180303 (Red Hat 7.3.1-5); Makefile OPTFLAGS -O3 -march=native, CFLAGS -std=c99, bench built with -std=c++11
hardware: Cannon Lake Core i3-8121U for the speedup table; cycles and MB/s tables also give Sky Lake Xeon W-2104 and Haswell Xeon E5-2697 v3
stars_or_usage: 57 stars; code of the paper 'Efficient Computation of Positional Population Counts Using SIMD Instructions' (Klarqvist, Muła, Lemire), Concurrency and Computation: Practice and Experience 33(17), 2021, DOI 10.1002/cpe.6304 (venue from search snippet; arXiv 1911.02696); README points production users to libalgebra
tradeoffs: Fastest variants need AVX-512 (Cannon Lake / Skylake-X class); SSE and AVX2 fallbacks are included; experimental repo, the README points production users to libalgebra.h; small arrays (under about 512 values) can be slower than the scalar path.
caveats: Speedup-table baseline is the compiler auto-vectorized scalar version at -O3 -march=native, a fair baseline; the 138.71x figure is against a deliberately non-vectorized baseline. Speedup table comes from one 2019-era laptop-class Cannon Lake CPU; the AVX-512 paths do not run on most AMD or client Intel parts of that era. The README tables predate the final code: the cycles and MB/s tables list methods (pospopcnt_u16_avx512_csa, avx2_csa, mula3) that no longer exist under those names in pospopcnt.c, and the speedup table's avx512_adder_forest/blend names are now avx512bw_*. Timing uses CPUID/RDTSC serialization per call and the input is regenerated and pre-touched by the reference function before each timed call, so small-array (128-512 values) ratios include fixed overhead and warm-cache effects. Peer-reviewed in CCPE 2021 (venue from search snippet only; arXiv not reachable). libalgebra (same author) reuses these kernels, so the two entries overlap; a follow-up paper (arXiv 2412.16370, Clausecker, Lemire, Schintke) extends the method to AVX2, AVX-512 and ASIMD.

name: Pure SIMD (pure_simd)
baseline: scalar_shader, the same per-pixel shader written as a plain scalar C++ loop in the repo's benchmark directory
workload: Per-pixel integer shader over a 512x512 int screen buffer (99 iterations of multiply and modulo-by-constant integer arithmetic per pixel), pure_simd_shader instantiated with vector sizes 1 to 128, against the same loop written in plain scalar C++.
claimed_speedup: Scalar 103 ms vs pure_simd width 64 10.9 ms (about 9.4x, derived from page data); width 32 12.5 ms, width 16 16.2 ms, width 8 28.0 ms; width 128 regresses to 158 ms (slower than scalar).
tradeoffs: No intrinsics: variadic-template unrolled vector types that rely on the compiler's SLP vectorizer (gcc or clang needed). Vector width must be tuned (too wide hurts the instruction cache). Header-only C++17; Conan is needed to build the tests and benchmarks.
caveats: A single toy workload (one shader adapted from the 'Practical SIMD Programming' tutorial) on one laptop CPU; the scalar baseline is the author's own loop with the same flags. Its inner loop is a serial 99-step dependency chain per pixel, so the gain comes from the compiler SLP-vectorizing the unrolled independent pixels, while the scalar loop as written evidently was not vectorized (it ties vector size 1 at 103 ms) and size 128 is 1.5x slower (158 ms). The shader relies on signed 32-bit overflow (px*py terms exceed INT_MAX), which is undefined behaviour in both versions; outputs match in the repo's test. The second benchmark (benchmark/sum.cpp) has no published results. Numbers are aggregate means of 10 repetitions. No comparison with Highway, xsimd, Eigen or std::simd; the README calls the library experimental with unstable interfaces.

name: xxhash-wasm
language: WebAssembly with JavaScript wrapper (implementation of xxHash 32-bit and 64-bit)
baseline: xxhashjs (pure JavaScript xxHash, uses cuint for 64-bit math); also Node built-in crypto md5 and sha1 (different, cryptographic algorithms)
workload: XXH64/XXH32 hashing via the public JS API. Third-party: byte-array one-shot (4 B, 8 B), 1 MiB bulk, streaming 1 MiB in 64 B-64 KiB chunks, and ASCII strings (8, 32 chars). First-party README: Benchmark.js ops/sec on random ASCII strings from 1 byte to 100,000,000 bytes, plus Node crypto md5/sha1 for comparison.
claimed_speedup: Third-party (haya32x64 docs/benchmarks.md, snapshot 2026-08-09, xxhash-wasm 1.1.0 vs xxhashjs 0.2.2, public API, medians of nine 150 ms samples): XXH64 one-shot 4-byte input 39.4 ns vs 1939.3 ns on C8a (AMD EPYC 9R45), about 49x (derived from page data), and 63.9 vs 2691.0 ns on C8g (Neoverse V2), about 42x (derived). 1 MiB bulk 15,973 vs 37 MB/s (about 432x, derived) on C8a and 10,738 vs 28 MB/s (about 384x, derived) on C8g. 8-char strings 59.2 vs 2437.8 ns (about 41x, derived). First-party README (Benchmark.js ops/sec): the prose says the 32-bit hash is up to 90x and the 64-bit up to 350x faster than xxhashjs. The table itself shows 32-bit from 11.2x at 1 byte (5,752,446 vs 513,517 ops/sec) up to 140.7x at 1,000,000 bytes, and 64-bit from 373x at 1 byte (4,438,501 vs 11,896 ops/sec) up to 677.8x at 100,000 bytes. At 100,000,000 bytes 64-bit is 34.56 vs 0.13 ops/sec (265.8x). All README ratios are derived from page data.
compiler_and_flags: Hand-written src/xxhash.wat built with wasm-opt --enable-bulk-memory -O4 (package.json build-wasm script; npm 1.1.0 artifact). Third-party run under Node.js 24.18.0 / V8 13.6.233.17-node.50 via node --expose-gc js.mjs (haya32x64 bench/, calibration plus warmup, then nine 150 ms samples, median). The first-party README table comes from bench/index.js (Benchmark.js, node --max-old-space-size=4096 index.js), with Node 17.3 stated for the Node-crypto table.
hardware: Third-party: AWS EC2 c8a.2xlarge (AMD EPYC 9R45) and c8g.2xlarge (Arm Neoverse V2), Ubuntu 26.04, timed work pinned to CPU 2. First-party README: an x64 MacBook Pro (CPU model not stated) running Node 17.3; the xxhash-wasm 64-bit column is identical in the xxhashjs and Node-crypto tables, so both appear to come from the same run (inference).
tradeoffs: Needs BigInt in WASM, bulk memory and TextEncoder.encodeInto (Chrome >= 85, Firefox >= 79, Safari >= 15, Node >= 15); older xxhash-wasm 0.4.2 is 3-4x slower. WASM instantiation takes about 1 ms in the browser and a little over 2 ms in Node. Small bundle (11.4 kB minified, 2.3 kB gzipped) versus xxhashjs 41.5 kB.
caveats: The baseline xxhashjs is a slow pure-JS port that emulates 64-bit math with cuint, not a tuned JS hash. The Node crypto comparison uses cryptographic md5/sha1. There is no native xxHash C baseline. The README prose (up to 90x/350x) understates its own table (up to ~141x/~678x, derived). In the first-party bench/index.js the xxhashjs calls also run .toString(16) on each result while xxhash-wasm returns raw numbers/BigInt, so the baseline does extra work (small at large inputs). Not the fastest wasm xxHash: hash-wasm 4.10.0's README shows XXHash64 at 101.66 MB/s vs xxhash-wasm 1.0.2's 47.58 MB/s at 32 bytes (2.1x, derived), with a tie at 1 MB (15,989 vs 15,929 MB/s). In haya32x64's harness, pure-JS haya32x64 (a different hash) beats xxhash-wasm XXH64 on 4-byte keys (22.9 vs 39.4 ns), and cyrb53 (53-bit) is faster still. The third-party measurer is a competing hash author's new repo (a wave-7 catalog entry), with one instance per host type. WebAssembly instantiation (~1-2 ms) is excluded. Needs BigInt-in-wasm, bulk memory and TextEncoder.encodeInto (Chrome 85+, Safari 15+, Node 15+).
